rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch, the business model, the chess expansion, and the pedagogy fight cleanly separated, then tells you exactly what proof would stop each one from becoming vapor. Its "Educators call gamified learning shallow. Duolingo's answer is a talking cartoon." is sharp but still honest about the outcome-data hole. B keeps walking past the evidence into thesis land: "pivoting from language app to AI learning platform" and "Replace a Human Tutor" are not in the update. That is how a founder ends up pitching a story the facts cannot carry.
gaps_in_A: "Profitable and growing 40%, Duolingo bets AI video justifies its priciest tier" — "priciest" is not supplied. Max is paid; the set correctly says to confirm pricing, but the headline still smuggles in hierarchy.
"it's a top-of-funnel move, not an upsell" — plausible, but still an inference. It needs Duolingo saying chess is acquisition strategy, not just a free course.

"Facts it rests on: a chess course launches free for all users; daily active users grew 40%" — the DAU stat gives scale, not proof that chess tests a broader learning platform. The angle is good; that support is a little loose.
gaps_in_B: "whether Duolingo is pivoting from language app to AI learning platform" — chess plus an AI video feature does not prove a pivot, and chess itself is not described as AI.

"The Question Is Whether It Can Replace a Human Tutor" — the update says conversation practice with Lily, not tutoring replacement. That comparison could be reported, but it is not grounded enough to lead.
"The nine-minute AI conversation session is a concrete counterpoint" — engagement time is not evidence against shallow-learning criticism. B knows this later, then commits the sin anyway.

"Why Duolingo Made Chess Free and AI Tutoring Expensive" — "AI tutoring" and "expensive" are both overstatements. The facts say paid Max subscribers get video calls; no price or tutoring claim was supplied.
